edited_rows.rationale: All rows of this psalm belong to a single parent unit. The title sits inside MT v1 (web:Ps.87.0 = oshb:Ps.87.1); its content opens oshb:Ps.87.1's “יְ֝סוּדָת֗וֹ בְּהַרְרֵי קֹֽדֶשׁ” (“His foundation is in the holy mountains”, web:Ps.87.1), names Zion as Yahweh's beloved city (web:Ps.87.2), and closes in direct address, oshb:Ps.87.3's “נִ֭כְבָּדוֹת מְדֻבָּ֣ר בָּ֑ךְ עִ֖יר הָאֱלֹהִ֣ים סֶֽלָה” (“Glorious things are spoken about you, city of God. Selah.”, web:Ps.87.3). This three-verse unit stands on descriptive/hymnic third- and second-person address to Zion, before the psalm's speaker shifts to first-person divine speech at web:Ps.87.4. Confidence is held at medium: at three verses this span sits near the whole-psalm threshold, and Psalm 87's terse, compressed style limits how firmly any internal seam can be argued from grammar alone.
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Treating Psalm 87's seven verses as one whole_psalm row is a live alternative given its brevity, but the shift from hymnic address about/to Zion (web:Ps.87.1-Ps.87.3) to first-person divine census-speech (web:Ps.87.4-Ps.87.7) is a genuine speaker change, not mere continuation.
observed_substrate_signals: oshb:Ps.87.1's opening clause carries its own expressed subject noun, יְ֝סוּדָת֗וֹ (‘his foundation’, a 3ms-suffixed noun), rather than lacking one; the title's “the sons of Korah” (web:Ps.87.0) names the psalm's authorship attribution, not this clause's referent
web_selah:true at Ps.87.3 (verse_map_web.json)
edited_rows.device_notes: The composition-level parent is Psalm 87 itself.

edited_rows.rationale: The closing strophe opens on first-person divine speech, oshb:Ps.87.4's “אַזְכִּ֤יר רַ֥הַב וּבָבֶ֗ל” (“I will record Rahab and Babylon”, web:Ps.87.4), following the Selah at web:Ps.87.3 (oshb:Ps.87.3). The WEB footnote glossing “Rahab” as Egypt is a translator's interpretive note, not a textual feature of oshb:Ps.87.4, and is disclosed here as such rather than argued as byte evidence. The register-list formula “This one was born there.” — oshb:Ps.87.4's “זֶ֝֗ה יֻלַּד שָֽׁם”, recurs, matching at the skeleton (consonantal) tier, at oshb:Ps.87.6's “זֶ֖ה יֻלַּד שָׁ֣ם” (web:Ps.87.6, sweep: 2 verses in Psalm 87, skeleton zeh yulad sham) framing web:Ps.87.5's variant “This one and that one was born in her;” before the unit closes on the communal declaration of web:Ps.87.7. Confidence is held at medium_low: the register-list genre and the Rahab identification carry real interpretive uncertainty, and the internal shape of this four-verse unit is argued from one repeated formula rather than a full set of tier-1 markers.
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Splitting the nations-register (web:Ps.87.4-Ps.87.6) from the closing communal declaration (web:Ps.87.7) into two rows is defensible given the Selah at web:Ps.87.6, but web:Ps.87.7's singers and dancers are naturally read as responding to the census just declared, not opening a new unit.
observed_substrate_signals: oshb:Ps.87.4 and oshb:Ps.87.6 match at the skeleton (consonantal) tier on the closing formula zeh yulad sham (raw/nfd/accent_stripped tiers do not converge)
web_selah:true at Ps.87.3 (front seam) and Ps.87.6 (interior)
the WEB footnote at web:Ps.87.4 identifying Rahab with Egypt is translator commentary, not verse text

edited_rows.rationale: The strophe opens immediately after the Selah at web:Ps.88.7 (oshb:Ps.88.8) on isolation from human companionship: “You have taken my friends from me” (web:Ps.88.8), “My eyes are dim from grief” (web:Ps.88.9). It moves into 3 verse-initial interrogative-he particles addressed to Yahweh about the dead (MT 88:11, 88:12, 88:13; 6 WEB question marks across web:Ps.88.10-Ps.88.12), opening oshb:Ps.88.11's “הֲלַמֵּתִ֥ים תַּעֲשֶׂה פֶּ֑לֶא” (“Do you show wonders to the dead?”, web:Ps.88.10, with Selah) and continuing web:Ps.88.11-Ps.88.12 (“Is your loving kindness declared in the grave?”, “Are your wonders made known in the dark?”) before the psalm returns to direct petition at web:Ps.88.13.
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Splitting the isolation report (web:Ps.88.8-Ps.88.9) from the rhetorical-question triad (web:Ps.88.10-Ps.88.12) into two rows is possible, but nothing marks a hard grammatical seam between them beyond a shift from statement to question.
observed_substrate_signals: web:Ps.88.10-Ps.88.12 carry 3 verse-initial interrogative-he particles (MT 88:11, 88:12, 88:13) about divine action toward the dead, rendered as 6 WEB question marks across the 3 verses (“Do/Is/Are…?”)
web_selah:true at Ps.88.7 (front seam) and Ps.88.10 (interior)

An undisclosed cross-seam envelope binds this row's own seam at web:Ps.88.12|Ps.88.13 to two verses outside it: web:Ps.88.8 = oshb:Ps.88.9 (הִרְחַ֥קְתָּ מְיֻדָּעַ֗י מִ֫מֶּ֥נִּי שַׁתַּ֣נִי תוֹעֵב֣וֹת לָ֑מוֹ כָּ֝לֻ֗א וְלֹ֣א אֵצֵֽא, ‘you have distanced my acquaintances from me’) and web:Ps.88.18 = oshb:Ps.88.19 (הִרְחַ֣קְתָּ מִ֭מֶּנִּי אֹהֵ֣ב וָרֵ֑עַ מְֽיֻדָּעַ֥י מַחְשָֽׁךְ, ‘you have distanced from me lover and friend, my acquaintances -- darkness’) share the same opening verb and the same noun, in reversed word order between the two verses

edited_rows.rationale: The closing strophe pivots on an adversative reopening of direct petition, oshb:Ps.88.14's “וַאֲנִ֤י אֵלֶ֣יךָ יְהוָ֣ה” (“But to you, Yahweh, I have cried”, web:Ps.88.13). It moves through renewed complaint (“why do you reject my soul?”, web:Ps.88.14) and terror imagery (web:Ps.88.15-Ps.88.17) to a final image of encirclement, closing on oshb:Ps.88.19's final word “מַחְשָֽׁךְ” (“darkness,” web:Ps.88.18): “You have put lover and friend far from me, and my friends into darkness.” No selah falls within this span, and the psalm ends on this word without any turn to praise or resolution within its own bytes.
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Reading web:Ps.88.13-Ps.88.18 as a continuation of the question-triad span rather than its own unit would miss the shift from interrogative address back to first-person petition at web:Ps.88.13.
observed_substrate_signals: oshb:Ps.88.14 opens with a fronted first-person pronoun (waani, an emphatic but-I opening) marking a return to direct address after the interrogatives of web:Ps.88.10-Ps.88.12
oshb:Ps.88.19's final word מַחְשָֽׁךְ (“darkness”) is the psalm's final byte, with no praise or resolution clause following it within the span

An undisclosed cross-seam envelope binds this row's own front seam at web:Ps.88.12|Ps.88.13 to a verse outside it: web:Ps.88.8 = oshb:Ps.88.9 (הִרְחַ֥קְתָּ מְיֻדָּעַ֗י מִ֫מֶּ֥נִּי שַׁתַּ֣נִי תוֹעֵב֣וֹת לָ֑מוֹ כָּ֝לֻ֗א וְלֹ֣א אֵצֵֽא, ‘you have distanced my acquaintances from me’), which web:Ps.88.18 = oshb:Ps.88.19 (הִרְחַ֣קְתָּ מִ֭מֶּנִּי אֹהֵ֣ב וָרֵ֑עַ מְֽיֻדָּעַ֥י מַחְשָֽׁךְ, ‘you have distanced from me lover and friend, my acquaintances -- darkness’, inside this row’s own span) answers in reversed word order -- same opening verb, same noun

edited_rows.rationale: The address shifts from the quoted oath back to direct praise of Yahweh: “The heavens will praise your wonders, Yahweh” (web:Ps.89.5) opens a doxological question — “who in the skies can be compared to Yahweh?” (web:Ps.89.6) — pursued through the council of the holy ones (web:Ps.89.7) to “Yahweh, God of Armies, who is a mighty one, like you?” (web:Ps.89.8). The preceding oath-citation closed under Selah at web:Ps.89.4 = oshb:Ps.89.5; this unit’s own content — the heavenly council’s incomparability question — is untouched by that closing mark and begins a new address.
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Running this unit through web:Ps.89.9 = oshb:Ps.89.10’s dominion-over-the-sea material was considered, but that verse trades the incomparability question (‘who is like Yahweh’) for a declarative act (“You rule the pride of the sea”), a different predicate class.
observed_substrate_signals: 3 WEB question marks over web:Ps.89.6-Ps.89.8 (Yahweh’s incomparability among the bene elim)
the heavenly council (sod qedoshim) as addressee-class shifts to declarative acts at 89:9

edited_rows.rationale: The hymn turns from the incomparability question to declarative acts of cosmic dominion: “You rule the pride of the sea” and “You have broken Rahab in pieces” (web:Ps.89.9-Ps.89.10), then creation itself — heavens, earth, north, south, Tabor and Hermon (web:Ps.89.11-Ps.89.12) — before the strength imagery of “Your hand is strong, and your right hand is exalted” (web:Ps.89.13) grounds the throne’s own foundation: “Righteousness and justice are the foundation of your throne” (web:Ps.89.14).
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Splitting the sea/Rahab pair (89:9-10) from the north-south creation list (89:11-12) as two rows was considered, but both develop the same declarative-act catalogue with no addressee or topic break between them.
observed_substrate_signals: declarative 2nd-person acts replace the interrogative mode of the preceding council question
the throne’s foundation clause (89:14) closes the catalogue of acts before the beatitude on “the people” (web:Ps.89.15) opens the next unit

edited_rows.rationale: The grammatical subject shifts at this row’s own seam: web:Ps.89.14 = oshb:Ps.89.15’s verbless clause, צֶ֣דֶק וּ֭מִשְׁפָּט מְכ֣וֹן כִּסְאֶ֑ךָ חֶ֥סֶד וֶ֝אֱמֶ֗ת יְֽקַדְּמ֥וּ פָנֶֽיךָ, is headed by the third-person nominal pair ‘righteousness and justice’ as its subject, with ‘your throne’ sitting inside the predicate’s construct chain as a possessive genitive rather than as the clause’s own subject; the beatitude that opens this unit, “Blessed are the people who learn to acclaim you” (אַשְׁרֵ֣י הָ֭עָם, web:Ps.89.15 = oshb:Ps.89.16), makes ‘the people’ the new nominal subject instead. Second-person address to Yahweh continues unbroken through the unit -- “They walk in the light of your presence, Yahweh” (web:Ps.89.15), “In your name they rejoice all day. In your righteousness, they are exalted” (web:Ps.89.16), and the unit’s own close “our shield belongs to Yahweh, our king to the Holy One of Israel” (web:Ps.89.18) -- so the seam is a subject-class shift (righteousness/justice to the people), not a break in addressee.
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Folding 89:15-18 into the preceding creation-hymn as one long unit was considered, but the grammatical subject moves from ‘righteousness and justice’ (the verbless clause’s own subject at the seam verse, web:Ps.89.14 = oshb:Ps.89.15) to ‘the people’, a fresh third-person nominal subject, a discourse-level shift; second-person address to Yahweh itself continues on both sides of the seam and does not mark it.
observed_substrate_signals: the beatitude’s own nominal subject, ‘the people’, replaces ‘righteousness and justice’ as the verse-initial grammatical subject at 89:15, while second-person address to Yahweh (‘your presence’, ‘your name’, ‘your righteousness’) continues unbroken through 89:15-89:17
the unit closes back on “Yahweh”/“the Holy One of Israel” (web:Ps.89.18) as the possessor of the people’s shield and king, returning to direct naming before the oracle opens

edited_rows.rationale: The psalm’s reversal opens on its own fronted, adversative pronoun: “But you have rejected and spurned. You have been angry with your anointed” (וְאַתָּ֣ה זָ֭נַחְתָּ וַתִּמְאָ֑ס הִ֝תְעַבַּ֗רְתָּ עִם מְשִׁיחֶֽךָ, web:Ps.89.38 = oshb:Ps.89.39). Direct second-person address to Yahweh, absent for the preceding 11 verses (oshb:Ps.89.28-Ps.89.38 = web:Ps.89.27-Ps.89.37, 0 second-person suffixes or independent pronouns across all 11), resumes at this unit’s own opening verse, but the mode inverts from oath-fulfillment to accusation: the covenant is renounced (web:Ps.89.39), the hedges broken (web:Ps.89.40), the adversaries exalted (web:Ps.89.42), and the anointed’s youth shortened “with shame” (web:Ps.89.45), corroborated by Selah at the unit’s own close (web:Ps.89.45 = oshb:Ps.89.46). The preceding oracle closed under Selah at web:Ps.89.37 = oshb:Ps.89.38, the front seam this unit inverts.
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Starting the lament one verse later, at 89:39, so that “you have rejected and spurned” (web:Ps.89.38) and “You have been angry” (web:Ps.89.38) split across two rows was considered, but both clauses share one verse (web:Ps.89.38 = oshb:Ps.89.39) and one fronted pronoun, and dividing one verse defeats the tiling rule.
observed_substrate_signals: ve-attah (‘but/and you’), a fronted independent pronoun with vav, opens a strong adversative at 89:38, tier-1

second-person address to Yahweh does NOT run unbroken into this unit: oshb:Ps.89.28-Ps.89.38 (=web:89.27-89.37, the preceding 11 verses) carry 0 second-person suffixes or independent pronouns; direct address to Yahweh resumes exactly at this unit’s own opening verse, oshb:Ps.89.39 (=web:89.38), while the mode flips from promise-fulfillment to accusation
Selah brackets the unit at both seams: web:Ps.89.37 = oshb:Ps.89.38 (front) and web:Ps.89.45 = oshb:Ps.89.46 (end)

edited_rows.rationale: The lament shifts from a series of accusing declaratives (“You have…”) to direct interrogative address: “How long, Yahweh? Will you hide yourself forever?” (web:Ps.89.46), moving through a meditation on mortality — “What man is he who shall live and not see death” (web:Ps.89.48) — to a closing plea that names the taunts “with which they have mocked the footsteps of your anointed one” (web:Ps.89.51). The preceding unit closed under Selah at web:Ps.89.45 = oshb:Ps.89.46, the front seam of this row; a further Selah falls inside this unit at web:Ps.89.48 = oshb:Ps.89.49.
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Treating the whole lament as one long row was considered, but “How long, Yahweh?” (web:Ps.89.46) opens a question-and-address mode distinct from the accusing “You have…” declaratives that precede it, and Selah marks a break at the seam between them.
observed_substrate_signals: interrogative address, עַד מָ֣ה (‘how long’, oshb:Ps.89.47 = web:Ps.89.46), replaces the declarative accusation series as the unit’s opening mode
Selah recurs at the front seam (89:45=46 MT) and again inside this unit (89:48=49 MT)

edited_rows.rationale: The psalm closes on the fixed book-boundary doxology formula: “Blessed be Yahweh forever more. Amen, and Amen” (בָּר֖וּךְ יְהוָ֥ה לְ֝עוֹלָ֗ם אָ֘מֵ֥ן וְאָמֵֽן, web:Ps.89.52 = oshb:Ps.89.53), baruch followed by amen x2. The formula answers nothing in the immediately preceding lament by content; it is the same closing class attested at the ends of Books I, II, and IV, marking the end of Book III’s collection (Psalms 73-89) rather than resolving the anointed one’s complaint.
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Folding this verse into the lament as its final line was considered, but the baruch-plus-double-amen formula shares its closing class with the book’s other book-boundary doxologies rather than continuing the lament’s own address to Yahweh in the second person.
observed_substrate_signals: baruch (‘blessed’) + amen x2 formula, matching in class the book I, II, and IV closing doxologies
the doxology stands outside the lament’s own second-person complaint address

edited_rows.rationale: The tefillah-le-Moshe title opens the psalm (תְּפִלָּה֮ לְמֹשֶׁ֪ה אִֽישׁ הָאֱלֹ֫הִ֥ים…, web:Ps.90.0 = oshb:Ps.90.1; the title sits inside MT verse 1, which also carries the prayer’s own opening line) and the unit states Yahweh’s eternity in two movements: relational — “Lord, you have been our dwelling place for all generations” (web:Ps.90.1) — then absolute — “before the mountains were born… וּֽמֵעוֹלָ֥ם עַד ע֝וֹלָ֗ם אַתָּ֥ה אֵֽל” (oshb:Ps.90.2), rendered “even from everlasting to everlasting, you are God” (web:Ps.90.2).
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Extending this unit through 90:3 was considered, but 90:3 turns from Yahweh’s own eternity to a direct statement about human mortality (“You turn man to destruction”, web:Ps.90.3), a new subject.
observed_substrate_signals: tefillah + le-Moshe title, the book’s only Moses-attributed superscription (sweep: 1 of 150 psalms; genre-label inventory), tier-1 opener
the unit’s content moves from relational dwelling-place language (90:1) to the fixed phrase ‘from everlasting to everlasting’ (90:2), both predicated of Yahweh/God
edited_rows.device_notes: One parent, Psalm 90, holds all of this prayer’s rows together as a single composition.

edited_rows.rationale: A causal connective binds mortality to divine wrath as its explanation: “For we are consumed in your anger. We are troubled in your wrath” (web:Ps.90.7) names sin as the cause (web:Ps.90.8) and totals the lifespan — “seventy, or even by reason of strength eighty years” (web:Ps.90.10) — before the unit closes on the wisdom petition its own meditation earns: “So teach us to count our days, that we may gain a heart of wisdom” (web:Ps.90.12).
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Carrying this unit through web:Ps.90.13 so that the wisdom petition and the plea to relent form one row was considered; both this unit’s own close and web:Ps.90.13 open on imperatives addressed to Yahweh (הוֹדַ֑ע, ‘make known!’, oshb:Ps.90.12; שׁוּבָ֣ה, ‘relent!’, oshb:Ps.90.13), so the seam is not reflection-to-imperative. The stronger warrant for keeping them apart is a root echo in reversed direction: וַ֝תֹּ֗אמֶר (‘return!’, oshb:Ps.90.3), Yahweh’s own imperative to ‘the children of men,’ is answered by שׁוּבָ֣ה (‘relent/return!’, oshb:Ps.90.13), the psalmist’s imperative back to Yahweh -- a role-reversal this unit’s own close (90:12) does not yet supply.
observed_substrate_signals: כִּֽי (‘for’, oshb:Ps.90.7) opens a causal connective tying the wrath-theme to the preceding transience images; standalone ki opens 3 verses in Psalm 90 (90:4, 90:7, 90:9), of which only 90:7 is this row’s own seam
the unit’s own close (90:12) is a request for wisdom, not yet the imperative petition series that follows

edited_rows.rationale: The psalm’s closing petition opens on a fresh imperative: “Relent, Yahweh! How long? Have compassion on your servants!” (שׁוּבָ֣ה יְ֭הוָה עַד מָתָ֑י…, web:Ps.90.13 = oshb:Ps.90.13), moving through the plea to be satisfied “in the morning with your loving kindness” (web:Ps.90.14) and for gladness proportioned to the years of affliction (web:Ps.90.15), to the psalm’s own final request, repeated for emphasis: “Establish the work of our hands for us. Yes, establish the work of our hands” (web:Ps.90.17).
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Splitting the petition at 90:15/16, separating the gladness-request from the work-of-our-hands request, was considered, but the volitive sequence -- 3 true 2ms imperatives (שַׂבְּעֵ֣נוּ ‘satisfy us,’ oshb:Ps.90.14; שַׂ֭מְּחֵנוּ ‘make us glad,’ oshb:Ps.90.15; כּוֹנְנָ֥ה ‘establish,’ oshb:Ps.90.17) framing one jussive-type passive (יֵרָאֶ֣ה ‘let it be seen,’ oshb:Ps.90.16, whose subject is ‘your work,’ not an addressee) -- runs without an addressee or mode break across the whole unit.
observed_substrate_signals: shuvah (‘return/relent’), an imperative opening a fresh petition at 90:13, echoes the shuvu (‘return’) addressed to ‘the children of men’ at 90:3, tier-2 verbal-root echo
the closing request (90:17) repeats ‘establish the work of our hands’ within the same verse for emphasis, the unit’s own final imperative

edited_rows.rationale: From web:Ps.91.3 the psalm addresses a singular 'you' directly, cataloguing dangers the addressee is protected from -- snare, pestilence, terror by night, the arrow by day -- through web:Ps.91.8, then restates the premise of that protection, “Because you have made Yahweh your…” (web:Ps.91.9), and its result, “no evil shall happen…” (web:Ps.91.10). This eight-verse span holds one continuous second-person address before a new governing image -- the angels of web:Ps.91.11 -- opens the next unit.
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: A break at web:Ps.91.9, where the refuge premise is restated, was rejected because vv.9-10 supply the reason and result for the preceding danger catalogue rather than opening a new topic; standalone ki opens 4 verses in Psalm 91 (91:3 כִּ֤י, 91:9 כִּֽי, 91:11 כִּ֣י, 91:14 כִּ֤י), 3 of which open this cluster’s own unit boundaries, but 91:9’s ki resumes the address already running since 91:3 rather than introducing a new grammatical subject or addressee the way the other three do.
observed_substrate_signals: the addressee is carried throughout vv.3-10 by second-person suffixed pronouns and, at 91:9, also by the independent pronoun אַתָּ֣ה (oshb:Ps.91.9, ‘you’), reinforcing rather than replacing the second-person address
web:Ps.91.10's closing clause answers web:Ps.91.9's premise within the same span
edited_rows.device_notes: No superscription or refrain marking touches this span, and no selah falls within it either; the danger catalogue forms one continuous address unit, distinct from the psalm's other spans.

edited_rows.rationale: web:Ps.91.11 introduces a new protective agent as the verb’s fronted object rather than the span’s grammatical subject: כִּ֣י מַ֭לְאָכָיו יְצַוֶּה לָּ֑ךְ לִ֝שְׁמָרְךָ֗ בְּכָל דְּרָכֶֽיךָ (oshb:Ps.91.11, 'for he will command his angels for you') keeps Yahweh, the 3ms referent already explicit at 91:3/91:9, as the verb’s subject, with מַ֭לְאָכָיו ('his angels', plural) as the fronted object/complement of the singular verb יְצַוֶּה; naming the specific agent of protection rather than the generic dangers of the preceding span; the angelic guardianship carries through web:Ps.91.13's triumph over the lion and serpent, before the voice shifts again to Yahweh's own first-person speech at web:Ps.91.14.
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: web:Ps.91.14 introduces a first-person divine speaker, a distinct voice from the third-person angels of vv.11-13, so carrying this span forward into it was rejected.
observed_substrate_signals: מַ֭לְאָכָיו (oshb:Ps.91.11, 'his angels') is plural while יְצַוֶּה (oshb:Ps.91.11, 3ms singular) is singular; number disagreement rules out the plural noun as the verb's subject, identifying it instead as the fronted object naming the protective agent, distinct from the implied dangers of the previous span
edited_rows.device_notes: The angelic-guardianship image is local to this span; it does not recur elsewhere in the psalm.

edited_rows.rationale: web:Ps.91.14 opens with the causal clause כִּ֤י בִ֣י חָ֭שַׁק וַאֲפַלְּטֵ֑הוּ (oshb:Ps.91.14, 'because he has clung to me and I will deliver him'), a first-person divine verb shifting the speaker from the address-voice of vv.3-13 to Yahweh's own voice; WEB marks the shift with its own quotation mark, opening “Because he has set his love on me,…” (web:Ps.91.14) and closing “…show him my salvation.” (web:Ps.91.16) at the psalm's end. This closing oracle, in which God speaks of the trusting individual in the third person ('him'), is a distinct unit from the second-person address that precedes it.
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Treating web:Ps.91.13 as the oracle's opening verse was rejected because it still addresses 'you' in the second person, while web:Ps.91.14 is where Yahweh's own first-person voice begins.
observed_substrate_signals: WEB brackets this span in its own quotation marks, opening at web:Ps.91.14 and closing at web:Ps.91.16, the psalm's final verse

the verb וַאֲפַלְּטֵ֑הוּ (oshb:Ps.91.14, 'and I will deliver him') is first-person, first-person divine speech -- Yahweh's own voice, distinct in speaker from the third-person and second-person address of the rest of the psalm, though not the psalm's only first-person verb -- 2 occurrences (אֹמַ֗ר/אֶבְטַח) recur at oshb:Ps.91.2, also 1cs
edited_rows.device_notes: The closing oracle carries the psalm's direct divine first-person speech, distinct in voice from its other three spans.

edited_rows.rationale: The title, מִזְמ֥וֹר שִׁ֗יר לְי֣וֹם הַשַּׁבָּֽת (oshb:Ps.92.1, 'a psalm, a song for the Sabbath day'), names this psalm for the Sabbath -- “A Psalm. A song for the Sabbath day.” (web:Ps.92.0) is the book's only WEB title to do so (sweep: 1 verse, book-wide 'Sabbath' search over WEB titles and text). Three infinitive clauses then open the body -- לְהֹד֥וֹת ('to give thanks', oshb:Ps.92.2) and וּלְזַמֵּ֖ר ('and to sing praise', oshb:Ps.92.2), both at web:Ps.92.1 = oshb:Ps.92.2, then לְהַגִּ֣יד ('to declare', oshb:Ps.92.3) at web:Ps.92.2 = oshb:Ps.92.3 -- with web:Ps.92.3 = oshb:Ps.92.4 as a verbless instrumental extension naming the instruments rather than a fourth infinitive clause, forming one syntactic unit that the causal 'For you, Yahweh' of web:Ps.92.4 breaks off from.
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: web:Ps.92.4 leaves the infinitive chain of thanksgiving-instructions for a direct second-person address to Yahweh, so extending this row through it was rejected.
observed_substrate_signals: the genre_label_membership inventory records this psalm under both mizmor and shir, matching the title's own two nouns

the psalm's 3 infinitives are לְהֹד֥וֹת/וּלְזַמֵּ֖ר (oshb:Ps.92.2) and לְהַגִּ֣יד (oshb:Ps.92.3); web:Ps.92.3 = oshb:Ps.92.4 (the ten-stringed lute, the harp, the lyre) is verbless, an instrumental extension of that chain rather than a third clause; all 3 verbal/instrumental elements are governed by 'It is a good thing' (web:Ps.92.1)
edited_rows.device_notes: Psalm 92 serves as parent for the rows it contains.

edited_rows.rationale: web:Ps.92.8 = oshb:Ps.92.9 opens with the adversative independent pronoun וְאַתָּ֥ה מָר֗וֹם ('but you, on high'), turning back to direct address after the wisdom reflection of vv.6-7; the enemies' perishing (web:Ps.92.9) and the psalmist's own exaltation and anointing (web:Ps.92.10) continue that address; the unit's own close, web:Ps.92.11, drops to first-person report ('my eyes...my ears') without renewing the second-person address, but stays inside the psalmist's own perspective; the fronted, unaddressed subject 'the righteous' at web:Ps.92.12 is what closes off the unit.
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Separating the enemies' perishing and exaltation (web:Ps.92.9-Ps.92.10) from the closing first-person report (web:Ps.92.11) was rejected because all 3 verses stay inside the psalmist's own perspective opened at web:Ps.92.8, without a fresh grammatical subject marking a seam until 'the righteous' at web:Ps.92.12.
observed_substrate_signals: וְאַתָּ֥ה מָר֗וֹם (oshb:Ps.92.9) is an explicit independent pronoun, distinct from the bound suffixes used elsewhere in the psalm
web:Ps.92.12 = oshb:Ps.92.13 opens with the fronted subject צַ֭דִּיק כַּתָּמָ֣ר יִפְרָ֑ח ('the righteous shall flourish like the palm tree'), a topic shift out of this row's address
edited_rows.device_notes: The horn-exaltation image (web:Ps.92.10) is local to this span. A byte-true verdancy link straddles the row seam at web:Ps.92.11|Ps.92.12: web:Ps.92.10 = oshb:Ps.92.11 (רַעֲנָֽן, 'fresh/luxuriant', singular, this span) and web:Ps.92.14 = oshb:Ps.92.15 (וְרַֽעֲנַנִּ֣ים, plural, the next span), singular/plural of the same adjective.

edited_rows.rationale: web:Ps.92.12 = oshb:Ps.92.13 opens with the fronted, unaddressed subject צַ֭דִּיק כַּתָּמָ֣ר יִפְרָ֑ח ('the righteous shall flourish like the palm tree'), leaving the second-person address of the preceding span for a third-person, gnomic image of the righteous planted in Yahweh's house (web:Ps.92.13) and still bearing fruit in old age (web:Ps.92.14); the psalm closes on the purpose clause “to show that Yahweh is upright.” (web:Ps.92.15).
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Keeping web:Ps.92.12 attached to the preceding span was rejected because it drops the second-person address entirely for a generalized class statement about 'the righteous,' a fresh grammatical subject rather than a continuation of 'you.'
observed_substrate_signals: the tree image (palm, cedar) and the temple-courts setting recur across vv.12-14 as one continuous figure, absent from the preceding span
edited_rows.device_notes: The closing verse's purpose infinitive, לְ֭הַגִּיד (oshb:Ps.92.16 = web:Ps.92.15, 'to declare'), repeats the opening infinitive לְהַגִּ֣יד (oshb:Ps.92.3 = web:Ps.92.2, also 'to declare') at the accent_stripped tier (a book-wide skeleton sweep of that spelling returns exactly 2 verses, both inside Psalm 92) -- a genuine repeated-wording inclusio pairing with web:Ps.92.2-Ps.92.3, not web:Ps.92.1. A byte-true verdancy link straddles the row seam at web:Ps.92.11|Ps.92.12 (this span's opening half): web:Ps.92.10 = oshb:Ps.92.11 (רַעֲנָֽן, singular, the preceding span) and web:Ps.92.14 = oshb:Ps.92.15 (וְרַֽעֲנַנִּ֣ים, 'fresh and flourishing', plural, this span), singular/plural of the same adjective. oshb:Ps.92.16's own closing purpose clause (quoted above) also carries one unrelated ketiv/qere note later in that verse (pmarks_Ps.json), not touching the infinitive quoted here.

edited_rows.rationale: The psalm opens “Yahweh reigns!” (web:Ps.93.1), the verb clause יְהוָ֣ה מָלָךְ֮ (oshb:Ps.93.1, 'Yahweh has become king') -- sweep: the skeleton יהוה מלך returns 6 verses book-wide (web:Ps.10.16, web:Ps.29.10, web:Ps.93.1, web:Ps.96.10, web:Ps.97.1, web:Ps.99.1), but the pointed verb מָלָךְ֮ (oshb:Ps.93.1), distinct from the noun מֶ֭לֶךְ (oshb:Ps.10.16, 'king', in 'Yahweh is king forever and ever'), narrows the 6 to 4 verses carrying the verb (web:Ps.93.1, web:Ps.96.10, web:Ps.97.1, web:Ps.99.1: sweep, 4 verses); web:Ps.93.1 precedes the other 3, making this the book's first YHWH-malak proclamation of the 4 (sweep, 4 verses). Five verses carry one continuous enthronement acclamation, from the throne 'established from long ago' (web:Ps.93.2) through the flood's roar (web:Ps.93.3-Ps.93.4) to the closing statement that “Your statutes stand firm.” (web:Ps.93.5); the address pattern forms an envelope across the whole psalm (5 verses): third-person acclamation opens it (מָלָךְ֮, 93:1), second-person address brackets its near side (oshb:Ps.93.2, כִּסְאֲךָ֣/אָֽתָּה), the flood imagery of 93:3-93:4 (2 verses) returns to third-person/impersonal description with no address of its own, and second-person address closes it again (oshb:Ps.93.5, עֵֽדֹתֶ֨יךָ/לְבֵיתְךָ֥) -- one indivisible unit built from that envelope, not from an unbroken absence of address.
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Splitting the psalm at web:Ps.93.2, separating the enthronement acclamation from the throne's antiquity, was rejected because the second-person address at oshb:Ps.93.2 (אָֽתָּה, an independent pronoun) is answered by the same address class again at the psalm's own close (93:5), an envelope bracketing the whole 5 verses rather than a seam opening a new unit; the flood imagery between them (93:3-93:4) carries no address of its own to mark a break.
observed_substrate_signals: מָלָךְ֮ (oshb:Ps.93.1) is a finite qal perfect verb, opening the psalm before any addressee is named

second-person address to Yahweh brackets the psalm as an envelope -- an independent pronoun at 93:2 (אָֽתָּה, oshb:Ps.93.2) and 2ms suffixes at 93:5 (עֵֽדֹתֶ֨יךָ/לְבֵיתְךָ֥, oshb:Ps.93.5) -- rather than running continuously or being wholly absent; no internal quotation marks a seam
edited_rows.device_notes: The psalm coheres as one composition -- parent grouping Psalm 93.

edited_rows.rationale: The psalm opens with an imperative appeal to the avenging God, אֵל נְקָמ֥וֹת יְהוָ֑ה (oshb:Ps.94.1, 'God of vengeance, Yahweh'), continuing in direct address through web:Ps.94.5 (עַמְּךָ֣/וְֽנַחֲלָתְךָ֥, 'your people'/'your heritage', oshb:Ps.94.5); the complaint then turns to third-person description of the wicked's deeds -- oppressing the widow, the foreigner, and the fatherless, named at web:Ps.94.6 -- and closes on their own quoted boast, “Yah will not see, neither will Jacob’s God consider.” (web:Ps.94.7). This seven-verse complaint ends before the imperative rebuke of the 'senseless' opens a new addressee at web:Ps.94.8.
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Ending the row at web:Ps.94.4, where the wicked's arrogant words are named, was rejected because their specific acts (vv.5-6) and their quoted boast (v.7) continue the same complaint without a new addressee or speaker.
observed_substrate_signals: oshb:Ps.94.1 opens with a doubled vocative, אֵל נְקָמ֥וֹת (oshb:Ps.94.1) named twice in the verse, an intensified invocation
the wicked's own words are quoted at the close of this span (web:Ps.94.7), not before it
edited_rows.device_notes: Psalm 94 supplies the parent for its strophes.

edited_rows.rationale: web:Ps.94.8 opens with the imperative בִּ֭ינוּ בֹּעֲרִ֣ים בָּעָ֑ם (oshb:Ps.94.8, 'consider, you dullards among the people'), addressing the senseless and the fools directly rather than Yahweh -- a wisdom-instruction register distinct from the preceding complaint. The rebuke's rhetorical questions (web:Ps.94.9-Ps.94.10) give way to a beatitude, “Blessed is the man” (web:Ps.94.12), on the man Yahweh disciplines, and the span closes on the promise that judgment 'will return to righteousness' (web:Ps.94.15); the rhetorical 'who' of web:Ps.94.16 then reopens the psalm in the first person, marking this eight-verse wisdom-instruction stretch as the psalm's internal seam between the opening complaint and the closing personal appeal.
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Splitting the rebuke of the fools (web:Ps.94.9-Ps.94.10) from the beatitude on the disciplined man (vv.12-15) was rejected because both remain in the same wisdom-instruction register; web:Ps.94.12 = oshb:Ps.94.12 does briefly address Yah directly (vocative + 2ms verb + 2ms suffix on 'your law'), but that address is localized to 94:12 alone and does not extend into web:Ps.94.13 = oshb:Ps.94.13, whose infinitive construct (לְהַשְׁקִ֣יט) carries no independent 2ms morphology of its own (0 instances across its own bytes), so it does not reopen the span's own general-audience register.
observed_substrate_signals: אַשְׁרֵ֤י (oshb:Ps.94.12, 'blessed') is a fixed macarism formula, not repeated elsewhere within this span
edited_rows.device_notes: The rebuke-then-beatitude pairing is a common wisdom-psalm move (the fool addressed, then the disciplined man blessed); it is texture within this span, not a further row boundary.

edited_rows.rationale: web:Ps.94.16 reopens the psalm in the first person, “Who will rise up for…” (web:Ps.94.16), a personal testimony -- Yahweh as help (web:Ps.94.17), comfort amid anxious thoughts (web:Ps.94.19) -- that gives way to direct second-person address to Yahweh already running by oshb:Ps.94.18 (חַסְדְּךָ֥ 'your loving kindness') and oshb:Ps.94.19 (תַּ֝נְחוּמֶ֗יךָ 'your comforts') and continuing at web:Ps.94.20's 'throne of wickedness' question, then closes on the psalm's final declaration, “Yahweh, our God, will cut them off.” (web:Ps.94.23). This eight-verse span carries the psalm from personal testimony to its concluding confidence, with no further addressee change strong enough to mark an internal boundary.
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Splitting this span at web:Ps.94.20, where the address turns back to Yahweh, was rejected because the surrounding first-person testimony (vv.16-19, 22) and the address to Yahweh (v.20) share the same complaint against 'the throne of wickedness' without a change of topic.
observed_substrate_signals: the standalone pronoun מִֽי (oshb:Ps.94.16, 'who') opens this span's rhetorical question; the preceding wisdom-instruction span (94:8-94:15) is itself built from interrogative-he questions (94:9-94:10) but carries 0 instances of standalone mi, which recurs 2x within web:Ps.94.16 alone -- the pronoun, not the interrogative mode generally, is what is new here

הַֽ֭יְחָבְרְךָ (oshb:Ps.94.20, an interrogative-prefixed verb bearing a second-person suffix) continues the direct address already running since 94:18-94:19, inside this span, noted as texture rather than a row boundary
edited_rows.device_notes: web:Ps.94.23 repeats its closing verb ('will cut them off') before naming 'Yahweh, our God,' an intensifying repetition distinct from the doubled 'God of vengeance' invocation that opens the psalm at web:Ps.94.1.
